claim: WILD-seq uses a lentiviral library to label cells with an expressed, heritable barcode that enables identification of clonal lineage in conjunction with single cell RNA sequencing.
source: WILD-seq uses a lentiviral library to label cells with an expressed, heritable barcode that enables identification of clonal lineage in conjunction with single cell RNA sequencing.
evidence: This is a direct description of the WILD-seq method from the manuscript text.

claim: The WILD-seq construct comprises a zsGreen transcript which harbours in its 3´ untranslated region (UTR) a barcode consisting of two 12 nucleotide variable regions separated by a constant linker.
source: The WILD-seq construct comprises a zsGreen transcript which harbours in its 3´ untranslated region (UTR) a barcode consisting of two 12 nucleotide variable regions separated by a constant linker (Figure 1a).
evidence: The manuscript describes the construct design and references Figure 1a which shows the lentiviral construct design.

claim: Each variable region is separated from any other sequence in the library by a Hamming distance of 5 to allow for library preparation and sequencing error correction.
source: Each variable region is separated from any other sequence in the library by a Hamming distance of 5 to allow for library preparation and sequencing error correction and we detected over 2.7 million unique barcodes in our vector library by sequencing after clustering based on Hamming distance.
evidence: This describes the design parameters of the barcode library.

claim: Over 2.7 million unique barcodes were detected in the WILD-seq vector library by sequencing after clustering based on Hamming distance.
source: Each variable region is separated from any other sequence in the library by a Hamming distance of 5 to allow for library preparation and sequencing error correction and we detected over 2.7 million unique barcodes in our vector library by sequencing after clustering based on Hamming distance.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from sequencing the barcode library.

claim: The barcode is appropriately positioned relative to the polyadenylation signal to ensure its capture and sequencing by standard oligo-dT single-cell sequencing platforms.
source: The barcode is appropriately positioned relative to the polyadenylation signal to ensure its capture and sequencing by standard oligo-dT single-cell sequencing platforms.
evidence: This describes the design rationale for barcode positioning.

claim: A WILD-seq barcode and clonal lineage could be unambiguously assigned to 30–60% of cells per sample within the presumptive tumour cell/mammary epithelial cell cluster.
source: A WILD-seq barcode and thereby clonal lineage could be unambiguously assigned to 30–60% of cells per sample within the presumptive tumour cell/mammary epithelial cell cluster.
evidence: This reports the efficiency of barcode assignment from the experimental data.

claim: A total of 132 different WILD-seq barcodes were observed in vitro.
source: A total of 132 different WILD-seq barcodes were observed in vitro and in total 94 different WILD-seq barcodes were observed across our in vivo tumour samples.
evidence: This is a direct count from the in vitro sequencing data.

claim: A total of 94 different WILD-seq barcodes were observed across in vivo tumour samples.
source: A total of 132 different WILD-seq barcodes were observed in vitro and in total 94 different WILD-seq barcodes were observed across our in vivo tumour samples.
evidence: This is a direct count from the in vivo sequencing data.

claim: The same clonal populations were reproducibly observed across animals and independent experiments.
source: We reproducibly observed the same clonal populations across animals and independent experiments which is critical to our ability to examine the effects of different interventions and treatments (Figure 1d and e).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1d and e demonstrating consistent clonal representation.

claim: The relative abundance of clones was similar in tumours grown in NOD scid gamma (NSG) immunodeficient and BALB/c immunocompetent mice but was drastically different to that found in the in vitro cell pool from which they were established.
source: The relative abundance of clones was similar in tumours grown in NOD scid gamma (NSG) immunodeficient and BALB/c immunocompetent mice but was drastically different to that found in the in vitro cell pool from which they were established (Figure 1e, Supplementary file 2), suggesting that clones that show greatest fitness in cell culture do not necessarily show fitness in vivo.
evidence: This is based on comparison of clonal proportions shown in Figure 1e across different conditions.

claim: Clones that show greatest fitness in cell culture do not necessarily show fitness in vivo.
source: The relative abundance of clones was similar in tumours grown in NOD scid gamma (NSG) immunodeficient and BALB/c immunocompetent mice but was drastically different to that found in the in vitro cell pool from which they were established (Figure 1e, Supplementary file 2), suggesting that clones that show greatest fitness in cell culture do not necessarily show fitness in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that clonal abundances differ between in vitro and in vivo conditions.

claim: The composition of the tumour microenvironment has a dramatic effect on the transcriptome of the tumour cells for all clones.
source: Pseudo-bulk analysis of the major clonal lineages revealed that the composition of the tumour microenvironment has a dramatic effect on the transcriptome of the tumour cells for all clones (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is based on pseudo-bulk analysis shown in Figure 1f comparing different microenvironments.

claim: Principal component analysis showed clear separation of tumour cells depending on their environment, with differences in interferon gamma signaling, TNF-alpha signaling, and cell cycle being most prominent between cells grown in vivo and in vitro.
source: Comparison of in vitro culture, tumours from NSG mice, and tumours from BALB/c mice by principal component analysis (PCA), showed clear separation of the tumour cells depending on their environment, with differences in interferon gamma signaling, TNF-alpha signaling, and cell cycle being most prominent between cells grown in vivo and in vitro (PC1, Figure 1g).
evidence: This is based on PCA analysis shown in Figure 1f and pathway analysis in Figure 1g.

claim: Differences in gene expression between tumours growing in immunocompetent and immunodeficient hosts were related to changes in the expression of extracellular matrix proteins and changes in interferon gamma and Il-2 signaling.
source: Differences in gene expression between tumours growing in immunocompetent and immunodeficient hosts were related to changes in the expression of extracellular matrix proteins and changes in interferon gamma and Il-2 signaling, consistent with the differences in T-cell abundance (PC2, Figure 1g).
evidence: This is based on PC2 analysis shown in Figure 1g.

claim: Clone 679 is the most distinct and the most mesenchymal of the clones.
source: Although there were large differences between clonal gene expression patterns across hosts, the clones showed consistent differences in gene expression across all settings, reflective of intrinsic clonal properties, with the biggest variation in gene expression across the clones being related to their position along the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) axis (PC3, Figure 1g). In particular, Clone 679 is the most distinct and the most mesenchymal of the clones.
evidence: This is based on PC3 analysis and EMT-related gene expression patterns.

claim: Treatment of 4T1 WILD-seq tumour-bearing mice with JQ1 caused an initial suppression of tumour growth but with only a small overall effect on time to humane endpoint.
source: Treatment of our 4T1 WILD-seq tumour-bearing mice with JQ1 caused an initial suppression of tumour growth but with only a small overall effect on time to humane endpoint (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is based on tumour growth measurements shown in Figure 2a.

claim: JQ1 treatment resulted in a reduction in Cd8+ T cells within 4T1 tumours.
source: When applied to our reclustered T-cells, Milo identified a significant decrease in abundance in cytotoxic T-cells, as identified by their expression of Cd8a and Cd8b1, following JQ1 treatment.
evidence: This is based on differential abundance testing using Milo shown in Figure 2c.

claim: JQ1 treatment caused significant down-regulation of a wide range of genes with consistent changes across clonal lineages.
source: As expected, given its mode of action, we identified significant down-regulation of a wide range of genes with consistent changes across clonal lineages (Figure 2d, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is based on differential expression analysis shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Among the genes repressed by JQ1 were a number of genes related to interferon (IFN) signaling and antigen processing and presentation, including Gbp2, Cd74, and B2m.
source: Among the repressed genes, were a number of genes related to interferon (IFN) signaling and antigen processing and presentation (Figure 2d and e), including Gbp2 which is strongly induced by IFN gamma, the MHC class II protein, Cd74, and B2m, a component of the MHC class I complex.
evidence: This is based on differential expression analysis shown in Figure 2d and e.

claim: JQ1 has been reported to directly inhibit transcription of IFN-response genes.
source: JQ1 has previously been reported to directly inhibit transcription of IFN-response genes (Gibbons et al., 2019; Gusyatiner et al., 2021) suggesting this may be due to the direct action of JQ1 within our tumour cells; however, JQ1-dependent changes to the tumour microenvironment may also influence these expression pathways.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Barcoded 4T1 clones showed varied sensitivity to JQ1, with treatment causing reproducible changes to clonal proportions within the tumour.
source: Our barcoded 4T1 clones showed varied sensitivity to JQ1, with treatment causing reproducible changes to clonal proportions within the tumour (Figure 2f and g, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on clonal proportion measurements shown in Figure 2f and g.

claim: Clone 473 was classified as highly sensitive to JQ1 treatment.
source: We classified one of the most abundant clones, clone 473, as highly sensitive to JQ1 treatment and three clones as being resistant to JQ1 treatment, clones 93, 439, and 264 based on these clones showing consistent behavior across two independent experiments (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1a for a side-by-side comparison of experiments).
evidence: This is based on clonal abundance changes across experiments.

claim: Clones 93, 439, and 264 were classified as resistant to JQ1 treatment.
source: We classified one of the most abundant clones, clone 473, as highly sensitive to JQ1 treatment and three clones as being resistant to JQ1 treatment, clones 93, 439, and 264 based on these clones showing consistent behavior across two independent experiments (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1a for a side-by-side comparison of experiments).
evidence: This is based on clonal abundance changes across experiments.

claim: JQ1-resistant clones which together make up less than 5% of the tumour in vehicle treated mice constitute on average 12.8% of the JQ1-treated tumours.
source: These resistant clones which together make up less than 5% of the tumour in vehicle treated mice constitute on average 12.8% of the JQ1-treated tumours.
evidence: This is based on quantification of clonal proportions in vehicle vs JQ1-treated tumours.

claim: Interferon signaling is highly correlated with sensitivity to JQ1.
source: Interestingly, interferon signaling which is significantly attenuated in our JQ1-treated tumours is highly correlated with sensitivity to JQ1, suggesting a possible higher dependence of the sensitive clones on these pathways.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis between baseline gene expression and JQ1 response.

claim: Resistance to JQ1 is associated with higher levels of unfolded protein response (UPR), in particular the IRE1 branch of the UPR.
source: Conversely resistance is associated with higher levels of unfolded protein response (UPR), in particular the IRE1 branch of the UPR (Figure 2h and i and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b), and mTOR signaling consistent with a known role of mTOR-mediated autophagy in resistance to JQ1 (Luan et al., 2019), and cytotoxic synergy between PI3K/mTOR inhibitors and BET inhibitors (Lee et al., 2015; Stratikopoulos et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 2h and i, and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Resistance to JQ1 is associated with higher levels of mTOR signaling.
source: Conversely resistance is associated with higher levels of unfolded protein response (UPR), in particular the IRE1 branch of the UPR (Figure 2h and i and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b), and mTOR signaling consistent with a known role of mTOR-mediated autophagy in resistance to JQ1 (Luan et al., 2019), and cytotoxic synergy between PI3K/mTOR inhibitors and BET inhibitors (Lee et al., 2015; Stratikopoulos et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Docetaxel treatment resulted in an initial, modest reduction in tumour growth followed by relapse in 4T1 WILD-seq tumour-bearing mice.
source: As with JQ1, docetaxel treatment resulted in an initial, modest reduction in tumour growth followed by relapse (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is based on tumour growth measurements shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Comparison of vehicle and docetaxel treated tumours revealed differential response of clonal lineages to treatment.
source: Comparison of vehicle and docetaxel (DTX) treated tumours revealed differential response of clonal lineages to treatment (Figure 3b, c and d, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on clonal proportion analysis shown in Figure 3b, c, and d.

claim: Clone 679 was classified as docetaxel resistant.
source: We classified clone 679 as docetaxel resistant and clone 238 as docetaxel sensitive based on these clones showing consistent behaviour across independent experiments (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1a for side-by-side comparison of experiments).
evidence: This is based on clonal abundance changes across experiments.

claim: Clone 238 was classified as docetaxel sensitive.
source: We classified clone 679 as docetaxel resistant and clone 238 as docetaxel sensitive based on these clones showing consistent behaviour across independent experiments (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1a for side-by-side comparison of experiments).
evidence: This is based on clonal abundance changes across experiments.

claim: EMT plays a major role in modulating sensitivity and resistance to taxane-based therapy.
source: This approach revealed a major role for EMT in modulating sensitivity and resistance to taxane-based therapy.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis between baseline transcriptomic profiles and docetaxel response.

claim: The 4T1 clones which are most sensitive to docetaxel are characterised by high expression of E-cadherin regulated genes and low ZEB1 activity consistent with a more epithelial phenotype.
source: The 4T1 clones which are most sensitive to docetaxel are characterised by high expression of E-cadherin regulated genes and low ZEB1 activity consistent with a more epithelial phenotype (Figure 3e and f, Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 3e and f.

claim: EMT and its associated endowment of cancer stem cell-like characteristics has been implicated as a mechanism of resistance to cytotoxic chemotherapies like docetaxel in cell culture and patients.
source: These observations are in agreement with previous studies that have implicated EMT, and its associated endowment of cancer stem cell-like characteristics, as a mechanism of resistance to cytotoxic chemotherapies like docetaxel in cell culture and patients (Bhola et al., 2013; Creighton et al., 2009; Gupta et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Resistance to docetaxel was highly correlated with up-regulation of genes whose expression is elevated in non-responders to docetaxel in human breast cancer patients.
source: This included genes whose expression is elevated in non-responders to docetaxel in human breast cancer patients (Honma et al., 2008) demonstrating the relevance of findings arising from this approach.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis and supported by citation to a patient study.

claim: Metabolic reprogramming is a potential mechanism of docetaxel resistance with higher expression of genes related to glycogen and glutathione metabolism being correlated with resistance to docetaxel.
source: Interestingly, we also identify metabolic reprogramming as a potential mechanism of docetaxel resistance with higher expression of genes related to glycogen and glutathione metabolism being correlated with resistance to docetaxel (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 3e.

claim: The response to docetaxel treatment in D2A1-m2 tumours was comparable to that observed for 4T1 tumours, with an initial reduction in tumour growth with subsequent relapse.
source: The response to docetaxel treatment was comparable to that observed for 4T1 tumours, with an initial reduction in tumour growth with subsequent relapse (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is based on tumour growth measurements shown in Figure 4a.

claim: In total 103 different WILD-seq barcodes were observed in vivo in D2A1-m2 tumours with a dramatic shift in relative clonal abundance on docetaxel treatment.
source: In total 103 different WILD-seq barcodes were observed in vivo with a dramatic shift in relative clonal abundance on docetaxel treatment (Figure 4b and d, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on barcode counting and clonal proportion analysis shown in Figure 4b and d.

claim: Unlike the 4T1 breast cancer model, variation between D2A1-m2 clonal lineages was no longer dominated by the EMT status of the clones and all clones exhibited a more mesenchymal-like phenotype.
source: Unlike our 4T1 breast cancer model, variation between clonal lineages was no longer dominated by the EMT status of the clones and all clones exhibited a more mesenchymal-like phenotype consistent with the fact that this was a subline of D2A1 selected for its metastatic properties (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is based on EMT gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Three D2A1-m2 clones (118, 2874, and 1072) were acutely sensitive to docetaxel, constituting on average 37% of vehicle-treated tumours but only 1.3% of docetaxel-treated tumours.
source: We identified three clones which were acutely sensitive to docetaxel, clones 118, 2874, and 1072. Together these constitute on average 37% of the vehicle-treated tumours but only 1.3% of the docetaxel-treated tumours (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is based on clonal proportion measurements shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Clone 1072 shows elevated levels of expression of cell cycle related pathways, such as E2F-target genes.
source: For example, clone 1072 shows elevated levels of expression of cell cycle related pathways, such as E2F-target genes (Figure 4f), indicating that aberrant cell cycle control in these cells could increase their susceptibility to an antimitotic cancer drug, interestingly high levels of E2F-targets have recently been shown to be associated with response to chemotherapy in breast cancer patients (Sammut et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4f.

claim: High levels of E2F-targets have been shown to be associated with response to chemotherapy in breast cancer patients.
source: For example, clone 1072 shows elevated levels of expression of cell cycle related pathways, such as E2F-target genes (Figure 4f), indicating that aberrant cell cycle control in these cells could increase their susceptibility to an antimitotic cancer drug, interestingly high levels of E2F-targets have recently been shown to be associated with response to chemotherapy in breast cancer patients (Sammut et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a patient study.

claim: Three D2A1-m2 clones (1197, 751, and 1240) robustly increased their relative abundance within the tumour following docetaxel treatment, making up less than 1% of vehicle-treated tumours but more than 20% of docetaxel-treated tumours.
source: Three clones robustly increased their relative abundance within the tumour following docetaxel treatment, clones 1197, 751, and 1240, which despite making up less than 1% of the vehicle-treated tumours together constituted more than 20% of the docetaxel-treated tumours (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is based on clonal proportion measurements shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Among the gene sets differentially expressed between resistant and sensitive D2A1-m2 clones were a number of breast cancer amplicons indicating that there may be specific copy number variations associated with these clones.
source: Among the gene sets differentially expressed between resistant and sensitive clones, were a number of breast cancer amplicons indicating that there may be specific copy number variations associated with these clones (Figure 4g and h).
evidence: This is based on gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4g and h.

claim: Gains in 8q24, 20q11 and loss of 16q have been reported to be associated with resistance to taxane-based chemotherapy.
source: Interestingly, gains in 8q24 (Han et al., 2010), 20q11 (Voutsadakis, 2021) and loss of 16q Höglander et al., 2018 have previously been reported to be associated with resistance to taxane-based chemotherapy in agreement with our findings.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Genes related to the NRF2 pathway were highly upregulated within all three docetaxel-resistant D2A1-m2 clones, even in the absence of docetaxel treatment.
source: Highly upregulated within all three of our resistant clones were genes related to the NRF2 pathway, even in the absence of docetaxel treatment (Figure 4g and h).
evidence: This is based on gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4g and h.

claim: NRF2 activation has been linked to cancer progression and metastasis and has been suggested to confer resistance to chemotherapy.
source: NRF2 activation has been linked to cancer progression and metastasis and has been suggested to confer resistance to chemotherapy (Homma et al., 2009; Jiang et al., 2010; Konstantinopoulos et al., 2011; Romero et al., 2017; Shibata et al., 2008; Singh et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Docetaxel had relatively little effect on the transcriptome of individual clones.
source: Consistent with their mode of action, docetaxel had relatively little effect on the transcriptome of individual clones (Figure 5a and b) while JQ1 caused substantial changes to the transcriptome predominantly down-regulating gene expression (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 5a and b.

claim: JQ1 caused substantial changes to the transcriptome predominantly down-regulating gene expression.
source: Consistent with their mode of action, docetaxel had relatively little effect on the transcriptome of individual clones (Figure 5a and b) while JQ1 caused substantial changes to the transcriptome predominantly down-regulating gene expression (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Genes were identified under all treatments that were altered within the tumour as a whole but as a result of clonal selection rather than intra-clonal changes in gene expression, with the biggest effects being observed with docetaxel treatment in D2A1-m2 tumours.
source: Genes were identified under all treatments that were altered within the tumour as a whole but as a result of clonal selection rather than intra-clonal changes in gene expression, with the biggest effects being observed with docetaxel treatment in D2A1-m2 tumours, in agreement with this condition inducing the largest changes in relative clonal abundance.
evidence: This is based on comparison of bulk vs clonal differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Genes upregulated only in bulk tumour analysis had significantly higher expression in clones resistant to chemotherapy.
source: As expected, we found that genes upregulated only in bulk tumour analysis had significantly higher expression in clones resistant to chemotherapy (that increase in abundance with treatment) and genes only down-regulated in bulk tumour analysis had significantly lower expression in these resistant clonal lineages.
evidence: This is based on baseline gene expression analysis shown in Figure 5d, e, and f.

claim: Genes only down-regulated in bulk tumour analysis had significantly lower expression in resistant clonal lineages.
source: As expected, we found that genes upregulated only in bulk tumour analysis had significantly higher expression in clones resistant to chemotherapy (that increase in abundance with treatment) and genes only down-regulated in bulk tumour analysis had significantly lower expression in these resistant clonal lineages.
evidence: This is based on baseline gene expression analysis shown in Figure 5d, e, and f.

claim: Among the genes that change in expression within the tumour as a whole as a result of clonal selection upon docetaxel treatment were a number of genes related to glutathione synthesis and conjugation including Mgst2, Esd, and Gclm.
source: Among the genes that change in expression within the tumour as a whole as a result of clonal selection upon docetaxel treatment, we identified a number of genes related to glutathione synthesis and conjugation including Mgst2, Esd, and Gclm (Figure 5a and b), that may endow resistant clones with greater ability to resolve reactive oxygen species (ROS) induced by docetaxel (Alexandre et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5a and b.

claim: In 4T1 tumours, Epcam was significantly reduced in expression in the bulk tumour but was not changed within the individual clonal populations.
source: Of note, we also observed that in 4T1 tumours, Epcam was significantly reduced in expression in the bulk tumour but was not changed within the individual clonal populations (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is based on differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Rather than inducing an EMT within the tumour cells, docetaxel is selecting clones of a pre-existing more mesenchymal phenotype.
source: This suggests that rather than inducing an EMT within the tumour cells, docetaxel is selecting clones of a pre-existing more mesenchymal phenotype.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Epcam changes in bulk but not within clones.

claim: 47 genes were identified as overlapping resistance genes between D2A1-m2 and 4T1 models.
source: We identified 47 overlapping resistance genes (Figure 6a, Supplementary file 12).
evidence: This is based on overlap analysis shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The 47 overlapping resistance genes were significantly enriched in pathways related to resolution of oxidative stress including the NRF2 pathway and glutathione-mediated detoxification.
source: These genes were significantly enriched in pathways related to resolution of oxidative stress including the NRF2 pathway and glutathione-mediated detoxification (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is based on gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The 47 gene taxane resistance signature is enriched in the clones from which it was derived (D2A1-m2 clones 1197,1240, 751 and 4T1 clone 679) but also enriched in 4T1 clone 439 after docetaxel treatment.
source: Further analysis of D2A1-m2 and 4T1 clones confirmed that our 47 gene taxane resistance signature is enriched in the clones from which it was derived (D2A1-m2 clones 1197,1240, 751 and 4T1 clone 679) but strikingly also enriched in 4T1 clone 439 after docetaxel treatment which was not used to derive the signature (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is based on gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6c.

claim: The 47 gene taxane resistance signature can de novo identify taxane resistant clones in the models.
source: These data suggest that our 47 gene taxane resistance signature can de novo identify taxane resistant clones in our models.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the signature identifies clone 439 which was not used to derive it.

claim: Expression of NRF2-target genes was a predictor of docetaxel resistance across the two models.
source: Given the enrichment for genes related to NRF2 signaling in our resistance gene signature, we also assessed whether expression of NRF2-target genes was a predictor of docetaxel resistance across our two models (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is based on gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Taxane-resistant D2A1-m2 clones 1197, 751 and 1240 are highly enriched for NRF2 signaling.
source: Analysis using an NRF2-target gene set from the ChEA database (Lachmann et al., 2010) across clones from D2A1-m2 confirmed our prior observation (Figure 4h) that taxane-resistant clones 1197, 751 and 1240 are highly enriched for NRF2 signaling.
evidence: This is based on gene set enrichment analysis using NRF2-target genes.

claim: Across 4T1 clones the only clone that showed enrichment for NRF2-target genes was clone 439.
source: Across 4T1 clones the only clone that showed enrichment for this gene set was clone 439.
evidence: This is based on gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6d.

claim: 4T1 clone 439 shows remarkable similarities to D2A1-m2 resistant clones, in that it shows high expression of NRF2-targets, has low abundance in vehicle-treated tumours and increases profoundly with docetaxel treatment.
source: This 4T1 clone shows remarkable similarities to our D2A1-m2 resistant clones, in that it shows high expression of NRF2-targets, it has low abundance in vehicle-treated tumours and increases profoundly with docetaxel treatment.
evidence: This is based on comparison of clonal characteristics across models.

claim: The human orthologs of the 47 taxane resistance genes were strongly enriched in human patient tumours following combined anthracycline and taxane-based therapy.
source: Importantly, the human orthologs of our 47 taxane resistance genes (Figure 6e, Supplementary file 12) as well as NRF2-target genes (Figure 6f) were strongly enriched in human patient tumours following combined anthracycline and taxane-based therapy, highlighting the potential clinical significance of our findings.
evidence: This is based on analysis of patient data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: NRF2-target genes were strongly enriched in human patient tumours following combined anthracycline and taxane-based therapy.
source: Importantly, the human orthologs of our 47 taxane resistance genes (Figure 6e, Supplementary file 12) as well as NRF2-target genes (Figure 6f) were strongly enriched in human patient tumours following combined anthracycline and taxane-based therapy, highlighting the potential clinical significance of our findings.
evidence: This is based on analysis of patient data shown in Figure 6f.

claim: Expression of both the 47 overlapping resistance gene set and the NRF2-target gene set was significantly increased after chemotherapy in human samples.
source: Expression of both these gene sets was significantly increased after chemotherapy, which our data would suggest is the result of outgrowth of resistant clonal lineages with increased propensity to withstand taxane-induced oxidative stress.
evidence: This is based on GSVA analysis of patient data shown in Figure 6e and f.

claim: Tumours with constitutively active NRF2, due to mutation in the negative regulator Keap1, have metabolic vulnerabilities that arise from their high antioxidant production, including dependency on glutamine and a general dependency on exogenous non-essential amino acids (NEAA) including asparagine.
source: To test this hypothesis, we leveraged the finding that tumours with constitutively active NRF2, due to mutation in the negative regulator Keap1, have metabolic vulnerabilities that arise from their high antioxidant production (Romero et al., 2017), including dependency of glutamine (Romero et al., 2017) and a general dependency on exogenous non-essential amino acids (NEAA) including asparagine (LeBoeuf et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: L-asparaginase is deployed in the clinical management of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and catalyzes the conversion of asparagine to aspartic acid and ammonia.
source: This metabolic dependency can be targeted therapeutically using L-asparaginase (ASNase from E. coli), which is deployed in the clinical management of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) (Batool et al., 2016), and catalyzes the conversion of asparagine to aspartic acid and ammonia (Chan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Treatment with L-asparaginase after docetaxel arrested tumour growth and led to a ~40% increase in time to endpoint in D2A1-m2 WILD-seq tumours.
source: As shown in Figure 7a, treatment with ASNase arrested tumour growth and led to a ~40% increase in time to endpoint (relative to vehicle) in this highly aggressive model, although the tumours did acquire resistance and regrew after approximately one week of treatment.
evidence: This is based on tumour growth measurements shown in Figure 7a.

claim: L-asparaginase alone had no significant effect on tumour growth in D2A1-m2 WILD-seq tumours.
source: Importantly, ASNase alone had no significant effect on tumour growth (Figure 7b), suggesting that docetaxel-dependent expansion of NRF2-high clones is required for ASNase treatment to induce a change in bulk tumour growth.
evidence: This is based on tumour growth measurements shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Docetaxel-dependent expansion of NRF2-high clones is required for L-asparaginase treatment to induce a change in bulk tumour growth.
source: Importantly, ASNase alone had no significant effect on tumour growth (Figure 7b), suggesting that docetaxel-dependent expansion of NRF2-high clones is required for ASNase treatment to induce a change in bulk tumour growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ASNase alone has no effect but ASNase after docetaxel does.

claim: Docetaxel-resistant D2A1-m2 clones 751, 1197 and 1240 exhibited a dramatic increase in their abundance with docetaxel treatment.
source: As before, our docetaxel-resistant clones, 751, 1197 and 1240, which have high levels of NRF2 signaling all exhibited a dramatic increase in their abundance with docetaxel treatment (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is based on clonal proportion analysis shown in Figure 7c.

claim: D2A1-m2 clones 751 and 1197 were sensitive to L-asparaginase returning to baseline levels.
source: Excitingly, clones 751 and 1197 were sensitive to ASNase returning to baseline levels.
evidence: This is based on clonal proportion analysis shown in Figure 7c.

claim: D2A1-m2 clone 1240 decreased in abundance in 2 of the 3 mice analysed and is likely to also be sensitive to L-asparaginase.
source: Clone 1240 decreased in abundance in 2 of the 3 mice analysed so is likely to also be sensitive to ASNase and further experiments confirm this (see below).
evidence: This is based on clonal proportion analysis shown in Figure 7c and further experiments.

claim: NRF2-high resistant clones were selectively targeted by amino acid deprivation as other clones such as 2323 were unchanged in their relative abundance.
source: As predicted, our NRF2-high resistant clones were selectively targeted by amino acid deprivation as other clones such as 2323 were unchanged in their relative abundance (Figure 7c and Figure 7—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is based on clonal proportion analysis shown in Figure 7c.

claim: Many of the genes found to be differentially expressed in tumour cells following L-asparaginase treatment are either directly related to protein synthesis or are consistent with changes in gene expression reported in cell lines following amino acid deprivation including Atf5, Atf3, Jun, Fos, Egr1, and Asns.
source: Many of the genes found to be differentially expressed in our tumour cells following L-asparaginase treatment are either directly related to protein synthesis (Eif3c, Gars, Eif3g, Eif5a) or are consistent with changes in gene expression reported in cell lines following amino acid deprivation including Atf5, Atf3, Jun, Fos, Egr1, and Asns (Fu et al., 2011; Pan et al., 2003; Pohjanpelto and Hölttä, 1990; Shan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on differential expression analysis shown in Figure 7d and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Asparagine synthetase (ASNS) was up-regulated following L-asparaginase treatment.
source: Of specific interest is the up-regulation of asparagine synthetase (ASNS) (Figure 7e) which catalyses the de novo biosynthesis of L-asparagine from L-aspartate and is therefore a potential mediator of ASNase resistance.
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis shown in Figure 7e.

claim: ASNS catalyses the de novo biosynthesis of L-asparagine from L-aspartate and is a potential mediator of L-asparaginase resistance.
source: Of specific interest is the up-regulation of asparagine synthetase (ASNS) (Figure 7e) which catalyses the de novo biosynthesis of L-asparagine from L-aspartate and is therefore a potential mediator of ASNase resistance.
evidence: This is based on known biochemistry and the observation of ASNS upregulation.

claim: In acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), low levels of ASNS resulting in a dependence on extracellular asparagine are considered an important biomarker for L-asparaginase treatment.
source: In acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), low levels of ASNS resulting in a dependence on extracellular asparagine are considered an important biomarker for L-asparaginase treatment.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ALL treatment.

claim: The importance of ASNS overexpression in conferring asparaginase resistance has been well documented and is frequently seen in ALL patients that develop drug-resistant forms of the disease following treatment with L-asparaginase.
source: Moreover, the importance of ASNS overexpression in conferring asparaginase resistance has been well documented and is frequently seen in ALL patients that develop drug-resistant forms of the disease following treatment with ASNase (reviewed in Richards and Kilberg, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: ATF4 is a well-known regulator of ASNS expression under conditions of amino acid deprivation.
source: The stress responsive transcription factor ATF4 is a well-known regulator of ASNS expression under conditions of amino acid deprivation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ATF4 function.

claim: There is a strong correlation between Asns and ATF4 activity across clones in L-asparaginase treated tumours (R=0.817, p=6.3 × 10–5).
source: AUCell analysis revealed a strong correlation between Asns and ATF4 activity across clones in ASNase treated tumours (Figure 7f. R=0.817, p=6.3 × 10–5) but not in vehicle (R=0.131, p=0.758) or DTX (R=0.397, p=0.158) treated tumours (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b), suggesting that ATF4 specifically drives asparaginase-induced Asns expression.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 7f.

claim: ATF4 specifically drives asparaginase-induced Asns expression.
source: AUCell analysis revealed a strong correlation between Asns and ATF4 activity across clones in ASNase treated tumours (Figure 7f. R=0.817, p=6.3 × 10–5) but not in vehicle (R=0.131, p=0.758) or DTX (R=0.397, p=0.158) treated tumours (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b), suggesting that ATF4 specifically drives asparaginase-induced Asns expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation being specific to ASNase treatment.

claim: Baseline Asns expression was consistent across clones and induction in response to asparaginase was observed across all clones analysed, suggesting a general resistance mechanism.
source: In our experiments, baseline Asns expression was consistent across clones and induction in response to asparaginase was observed across all clones analysed, albeit to slightly different magnitudes, (Figure 7e) suggesting a general resistance mechanism and supporting the clinical utility of an ASNS inhibitor, if one were to be developed, as third line treatment in this context.
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis shown in Figure 7e.

claim: Monoclonal tumours derived from D2A1-m2 clone 751 or 1240 both exhibited significant suppression of tumour growth in response to L-asparaginase monotherapy.
source: As shown in Figure 7g, monoclonal tumours derived from clone 751 or 1240 both exhibited significant suppression of tumour growth in response to ASNase (Figure 7g), while tumours derived from our standard 3 pools of D2A1-m2 WILD-seq cells containing all clones (Figure 7g) did not.
evidence: This is based on tumour growth measurements shown in Figure 7g.

claim: Tumours derived from the standard 3 pools of D2A1-m2 WILD-seq cells containing all clones did not exhibit suppression of tumour growth in response to L-asparaginase monotherapy.
source: As shown in Figure 7g, monoclonal tumours derived from clone 751 or 1240 both exhibited significant suppression of tumour growth in response to ASNase (Figure 7g), while tumours derived from our standard 3 pools of D2A1-m2 WILD-seq cells containing all clones (Figure 7g) did not.
evidence: This is based on tumour growth measurements shown in Figure 7g.

claim: NRF2-high clones have a pre-existing sensitivity to L-asparaginase and docetaxel treatment merely increases their abundance rather than shaping their phenotype.
source: These data strongly indicate that NRF2-high clones have a pre-existing sensitivity to ASNase and that docetaxel treatment merely increases their abundance rather than shaping their phenotype.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that monoclonal tumours are sensitive to ASNase without prior docetaxel exposure.

claim: WILD-seq can identify causal mechanisms of drug resistance in vivo that can be leveraged to inform new combination therapies.
source: In summary, our data support the notion that WILD-seq can identify causal mechanisms of drug resistance in vivo, that can be leveraged to inform new combination therapies.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the entire study.

claim: The redox defense signatures identified are detectable in patients after neo-adjuvant chemotherapy (NAC).
source: Since the redox defense signatures we identified are detectable in patients after neo-adjuvant chemotherapy (NAC), one can envisage an approach whereby patients receiving NAC have the surgical tumour specimen profiled for NRF2 gene signatures and those with high levels receive a post-operative course of L-asparaginase.
evidence: This is based on analysis of patient data shown in Figure 6e and f.

claim: Tumour heterogeneity is thought to underlie drug resistance through the selection of clonal lineages that can preferentially survive therapy.
source: Tumour heterogeneity is thought to underlie drug resistance through the selection of clonal lineages that can preferentially survive therapy.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific understanding.

claim: WILD-seq is a system that leverages expressed barcodes, population bottle necking, syngeneic mouse models and single cell RNA-seq to link clonal lineage to the transcriptome.
source: To overcome these challenges, we developed WILD-seq, a system that leverages expressed barcodes, population bottle necking, syngeneic mouse models and single cell RNA-seq to link clonal lineage to the transcriptome.
evidence: This is a description of the WILD-seq method.

claim: WILD-seq purposefully bottlenecks the clonal population to achieve a balance between maximising clonal diversity and minimising variation in clonal representation across replicate animals and experiments.
source: Our approach is unique in that we purposefully bottleneck our clonal population to achieve a balance between maximising clonal diversity and minimising variation in clonal representation across replicate animals and experiments.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the WILD-seq approach.

claim: The bottlenecking feature of WILD-seq allows robust calling of clonal gene expression signatures and differential clonal abundance before and after therapeutic intervention.
source: It is this feature that allows us to robustly call clonal gene expression signatures and differential clonal abundance before and after therapeutic intervention and it is this in turn that allows us to identify relevant drug resistance mechanisms in vivo.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the bottlenecking approach.

claim: The abundance of clones in cell culture and in vivo differ greatly, with the most abundant clones in vitro being lowly represented in vivo and vice versa.
source: We find that the abundance of clones in cell culture and in vivo differ greatly, with the most abundant clones in vitro being lowly represented in vivo and vice versa thus providing a cautionary note when analyzing drug response in vitro.
evidence: This is based on comparison of clonal abundances shown in Figure 1e.

claim: WILD-seq of 4T1 tumours revealed that the relative immune competence of the host profoundly sculpts the transcriptome of clonal lineages.
source: Moreover, WILD-seq of 4T1 tumours revealed that the relative immune competence of the host profoundly sculpts the transcriptome of clonal lineages and, as exemplified by JQ1, therapeutic interventions can impact the tumour microenvironment and its interaction with tumour cells, effects that would be missed in vitro and in immunocompromised hosts.
evidence: This is based on PCA analysis shown in Figure 1f and g.

claim: Therapeutic interventions can impact the tumour microenvironment and its interaction with tumour cells, effects that would be missed in vitro and in immunocompromised hosts.
source: Moreover, WILD-seq of 4T1 tumours revealed that the relative immune competence of the host profoundly sculpts the transcriptome of clonal lineages and, as exemplified by JQ1, therapeutic interventions can impact the tumour microenvironment and its interaction with tumour cells, effects that would be missed in vitro and in immunocompromised hosts.
evidence: This is based on observations from JQ1 treatment shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Over the time frames examined, clonal selection is the dominant force driving resistance to taxane chemotherapy in the 4T1 and D2A1-m2 models.
source: Our data with docetaxel treatment in the 4T1 and D2A1-m2 models indicate that, over the time frames we have examined, clonal selection is the dominant force driving resistance to taxane chemotherapy, with gene expression signatures, such as EMT and NRF2 signaling, being present in clones at baseline that are then selected for during therapy.
evidence: This is based on comparison of bulk vs clonal analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Gene expression signatures such as EMT and NRF2 signaling are present in clones at baseline and are then selected for during taxane therapy.
source: Our data with docetaxel treatment in the 4T1 and D2A1-m2 models indicate that, over the time frames we have examined, clonal selection is the dominant force driving resistance to taxane chemotherapy, with gene expression signatures, such as EMT and NRF2 signaling, being present in clones at baseline that are then selected for during therapy.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Monoclonal tumours derived from NRF2-high D2A1-m2 clones are inherently sensitive to L-asparaginase without ever having been exposed to taxanes.
source: Critical support for a clonal selection mechanism comes from the observation that monoclonal tumours derived from NRF2-high D2A1-m2 clones are inherently sensitive to L-asparaginase without ever having been exposed to taxanes, indicating that docetaxel merely enriches for these clones that have a pre-existing vulnerability to asparagine deprivation.
evidence: This is based on tumour growth measurements shown in Figure 7g.

claim: Up-regulation of Asns after L-asparaginase treatment is suggestive of an adaptive transcriptional resistance phenotype.
source: Conversely, up-regulation of Asns, which was detected across clonal lineages after L-asparaginase treatment, is suggestive of an adaptive transcriptional resistance phenotype.
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis shown in Figure 7e.

claim: Depending on the mode of action of specific drugs, transcriptional reprogramming may also induce therapeutic resistance and such mechanisms can be effectively identified with the WILD-seq platform.
source: Therefore, depending on the mode of action of specific drugs, transcriptional reprogramming may also induce therapeutic resistance and such mechanisms can also be effectively identified with the WILD-seq platform where clonal resolution can confirm a lack of clonal selection.
evidence: This is a general conclusion based on the observations with ASNase.

claim: The shift towards a more mesenchymal tumour phenotype upon taxane treatment is driven by clonal selection rather than a change in the state of cells.
source: While the data presented here suggest that the shift towards a more mesenchymal tuour phenotype upon taxane treatment is driven by clonal selection rather than a change in the state of cells, it is entirely plausible that transient changes in EMT status occur within our clonal population that are missed by sampling at endpoint.
evidence: This is based on the observation that Epcam changes in bulk but not within clones (Figure 5b).

claim: Overlapping resistance genes for docetaxel across two TNBC models uncovered a critical role for redox defense in docetaxel resistance that also appears to be operative in human breast cancer patients after chemotherapy.
source: Applying WILD-seq to examine docetaxel response across two TNBC models afforded the opportunity to overlap resistance genes for the same drug across models and remove model-specific effects. These analyses uncovered a critical role for redox defense in docetaxel resistance that also appears to be operative in human breast cancer patients after chemotherapy.
evidence: This is based on overlap analysis shown in Figure 6 and patient data analysis.

claim: Collateral sensitivity is the phenomenon by which resistance to one drug comes at the cost of sensitivity to a second drug.
source: Collateral sensitivity, first described for antibiotics (Imamovic and Sommer, 2013; Pluchino et al., 2012; Roemhild and Andersson, 2021) is the phenomenon by which resistance to one drug comes at the cost of sensitivity to a second drug.
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Application of L-asparaginase after docetaxel treatment led to an initial cessation of tumour growth followed by regrowth 6 days later.
source: Application of L-asparaginase after docetaxel treatment led to an initial cessation of tumour growth followed by regrowth 6 days later.
evidence: This is based on tumour growth measurements shown in Figure 7a.

claim: WILD-seq of docetaxel-treated tumours before and after L-asparaginase treatment confirmed the specific suppression of NRF2-high clones.
source: WILD-seq of docetaxel-treated tumours before and after L-asparaginase treatment confirmed the specific suppression of NRF2-high clones and also revealed a compensatory, largely clone agnostic, up-regulation of asparagine synthetase (Asns), which likely drives relapse in these tumours given the importance of ASNS to L-asparaginase resistance in ALL (Richards and Kilberg, 2006).
evidence: This is based on clonal proportion analysis shown in Figure 7c.

claim: A compensatory, largely clone agnostic, up-regulation of asparagine synthetase (Asns) likely drives relapse after L-asparaginase treatment.
source: WILD-seq of docetaxel-treated tumours before and after L-asparaginase treatment confirmed the specific suppression of NRF2-high clones and also revealed a compensatory, largely clone agnostic, up-regulation of asparagine synthetase (Asns), which likely drives relapse in these tumours given the importance of ASNS to L-asparaginase resistance in ALL (Richards and Kilberg, 2006).
evidence: This is inferred from gene expression analysis shown in Figure 7e and supported by citation to ALL literature.

claim: Asparagine bioavailability regulates EMT and metastatic progression in breast cancer models.
source: Interestingly, we have previously shown that asparagine bioavailability regulates EMT and metastatic progression in breast cancer models (Knott et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Asparagine deprivation may present multiple benefits to breast cancer patients and the utility of L-asparaginase in this setting warrants further investigation.
source: Thus, asparagine deprivation, which has not been extensively explored in breast cancer, may present multiple benefits to patients and the utility of L-asparaginase, a clinical stage drug, in this setting warrants further investigation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: Cells can supply themselves with asparagine through three avenues: (1) uptake of extracellular asparagine, (2) de novo synthesis through Asns, or (3) catabolism of existing proteins.
source: Nevertheless, hope still remains since there are only three avenues by which cells can supply themselves with asparagine (1) uptake of extracellular asparagine which is effectively shut-off by ASNase (2) de novo synthesis through Asns or (3) catabolism of existing proteins.
evidence: This is based on established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Forcing tumours to depend on synthesis through ASNS and then depriving them of that dependency with ASNS-directed therapeutics may provide a general approach to achieving durable therapeutic responses.
source: If we could effectively force tumours to depend on synthesis through ASNS, we could then deprive them of that additional dependency if ASNS-directed therapeutics were to be developed. This concept of steering clonal evolution with drugs towards a predictable and irreconcilable, therapeutically targetable, dependency may provide a general approach to achieving durable therapeutic responses for which tractable models of tumour evolution, such as those described here, are essential predictive components.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the findings.

claim: Intra-tumoural heterogeneity (ITH) is thought to underlie tumour progression and resistance to therapy by providing a reservoir of phenotypically diverse clonal lineages on which selective pressures exert their effects.
source: Intra-tumoural heterogeneity (ITH) is thought to underlie tumour progression and resistance to therapy by providing a reservoir of phenotypically diverse clonal lineages on which selective pressures from the microenvironment or therapeutic intervention exert their effects (Bhang et al., 2015; Turajlic and Swanton, 2016).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific understanding supported by citations.

claim: Inference of clonal composition from bulk sequencing has elucidated the breadth of ITH across tumour types and suggests that often rare pre-existing clones can resist therapy-induced killing to drive relapse.
source: Inference of clonal composition from bulk sequencing has elucidated the breadth of ITH across tumour types and suggests that often rare pre-existing clones can resist therapy-induced killing to drive relapse (Dentro et al., 2021; Ding et al., 2012; Gerlinger et al., 2012; Jamal-Hanjani et al., 2014; Landau et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Bulk sequencing methods are limited by their inability to characterise resistant clones beyond genotype and how their properties change over time and in response to therapy.
source: However, such methods are limited by their inability to characterise such resistant clones beyond genotype and how their properties change over time and in response to therapy.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of bulk sequencing methods.

claim: Several lineage tracing approaches have emerged that are able to link clonal identity with gene expression by utilising expressed genetic barcodes that are read-out by single cell RNA sequencing.
source: Recently, several lineage tracing approaches have emerged that are able to link clonal identity with gene expression by utilising expressed genetic barcodes that are read-out by single cell RNA sequencing (Biddy et al., 2018; Gutierrez et al., 2021; Quinn et al., 2021; Simeonov et al., 2021; Weinreb et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: To date in solid tumours, lineage tracing technologies have mostly been used to study drug response in vitro or metastatic dissemination in vivo and have not been utilised to study therapeutic response in immune-competent models.
source: However, to date in solid tumours these technologies have mostly been used to study drug response in vitro (Gutierrez et al., 2021; Oren et al., 2021) or metastatic dissemination in vivo (Quinn et al., 2021; Simeonov et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2022) and have not been utilised to study therapeutic response in immune-competent models.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Most existing combination cancer therapies are not rationally designed but were instead empirically optimised to avoid overlapping toxicities.
source: Most existing combination cancer therapies are not rationally designed but were instead empirically optimised to avoid overlapping toxicities.
evidence: This is a statement about current cancer therapy approaches.

claim: Alternative therapeutic strategies have emerged including synthetic lethality, drug synergy, and collateral sensitivity that aim to leverage selective vulnerabilities of tumour cells while minimising toxicity.
source: More recently alternative therapeutic strategies have emerged including synthetic lethality, drug synergy (AlLazikani et al., 2012; ONeil et al., 2017), and collateral sensitivity (Mueller et al., 2021; Pluchino et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2016) that aim to leverage selective vulnerabilities of tumour cells while minimising toxicity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The identification of frontline therapy-induced collateral sensitivities to second line therapy would have the potential to be rapidly translated into improved outcomes for patients.
source: Since many modern clinical trials occur in the context of neo-adjuvant chemotherapy, the identification of frontline therapy-induced collateral sensitivities to second line therapy would have the potential to be rapidly translated into improved outcomes for patients.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential clinical impact of identifying collateral sensitivities.

claim: Analysis of response of TNBC models to frontline taxane-based chemotherapy revealed an enrichment of clones with high levels of NRF2 signaling, implicating defense against oxidative damage as a major determinant of resistance to chemotherapy.
source: Importantly, analysis of response of TNBC models to frontline taxane-based chemotherapy revealed an enrichment of clones with high levels of NRF2 signaling, implicating defense against oxidative damage as a major determinant of resistance to chemotherapy.
evidence: This is based on the findings shown in Figures 4, 5, and 6.

claim: NRF2-high, taxane-resistant lineages are collaterally sensitive to asparagine deprivation as a result of L-asparaginase treatment.
source: Building on the work of others (LeBoeuf et al., 2020), we show that these NRF2-high, taxane-resistant lineages are collaterally sensitive to asparagine deprivation as a result of L-asparaginase treatment and that they adapt to this second line intervention by up-regulating de novo asparagine synthesis by increasing asparagine synthetase (Asns) expression.
evidence: This is based on the findings shown in Figure 7.

claim: NRF2-high, taxane-resistant lineages adapt to L-asparaginase treatment by up-regulating de novo asparagine synthesis by increasing asparagine synthetase (Asns) expression.
source: Building on the work of others (LeBoeuf et al., 2020), we show that these NRF2-high, taxane-resistant lineages are collaterally sensitive to asparagine deprivation as a result of L-asparaginase treatment and that they adapt to this second line intervention by up-regulating de novo asparagine synthesis by increasing asparagine synthetase (Asns) expression.
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis shown in Figure 7e.

claim: High levels of NRF2 signaling, which is also observed in patients following neo-adjuvant chemotherapy, promotes both resistance to chemotherapy and sensitivity to asparagine deprivation.
source: Together these data indicate that high levels of NRF2 signaling, which is also observed in patients following neo-adjuvant chemotherapy, promotes both resistance to chemotherapy and sensitivity to asparagine deprivation and warrant the exploration of L-asparaginase as a therapeutic modality in solid tumours.
evidence: This is based on the findings from mouse models and patient data analysis.

claim: The findings warrant the exploration of L-asparaginase as a therapeutic modality in solid tumours.
source: Together these data indicate that high levels of NRF2 signaling, which is also observed in patients following neo-adjuvant chemotherapy, promotes both resistance to chemotherapy and sensitivity to asparagine deprivation and warrant the exploration of L-asparaginase as a therapeutic modality in solid tumours.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of the study.
